workflow_configuration.task_objective: Architect and deliver a production-grade desktop application in Python or Rust that pairs a rich, responsive GUI with a fully decoupled asynchronous core. The architectural goal is strict unidirectional data flow: an immutable-by-default domain model, a single authoritative state store, and a UI layer that is a pure projection of state. Performance standards: sustained 60 FPS render loop (frame budget 16.6 ms, main thread never blocked longer than 4 ms by application code); cold start under 1.5 s; UI-perceived latency under 100 ms for all interactive operations, with anything longer delegated to background workers and surfaced via progress state; steady-state memory flat under soak testing (zero unbounded growth over 24 h); graceful degradation and cancellation for all long-running operations. The system must be deterministic under test: every business rule reachable and verifiable without instantiating any UI component.

system_requirements.language_selection: Choose Rust when memory safety, binary distribution, and predictable latency dominate; choose Python when iteration speed and ecosystem breadth (data, ML, scientific) dominate. Do not mix at the UI boundary; if both are needed, isolate Rust as a PyO3/maturin extension module beneath a Python shell.

ui_frameworks.python: PySide6/Qt 6 (QML for rich composited UI, Widgets for dense desktop tooling); acceptable alternative: Dear PyGui for immediate-mode tooling UIs.
ui_frameworks.rust: Primary: Tauri 2 (webview shell, Rust core) for rich product UI; egui/eframe for immediate-mode tooling; Slint or Iced for declarative retained-mode native UI.

concurrency_models.python: asyncio event loop for I/O-bound orchestration, bridged to Qt via qasync; concurrent.futures.ProcessPoolExecutor for CPU-bound work (GIL bypass); QThreadPool/QRunnable only for Qt-object-adjacent background tasks; all cross-thread UI mutation exclusively via queued signal/slot connections.
concurrency_models.rust: tokio multi-threaded runtime for async I/O; rayon for data-parallel CPU work; dedicated UI thread owned by the framework; cross-thread communication via bounded tokio::sync::mpsc / watch channels; shared state via Arc with interior mutability limited to RwLock/Mutex at the store boundary, never scattered through domain types.

core_dependencies.python: pydantic v2 (validated domain models), attrs/dataclasses (frozen value objects), qasync, structlog, pytest + pytest-asyncio + pytest-qt + hypothesis, mypy --strict, ruff, uv for lockfile-based dependency pinning.
core_dependencies.rust: serde + serde_json (serialization), thiserror (library errors) + anyhow (application errors only at the shell), tracing + tracing-subscriber (structured telemetry), tokio, rayon, proptest, criterion (benchmarks), cargo-deny (license/advisory audit), clippy with -D warnings.

system_requirements.build_and_distribution: Reproducible builds from a committed lockfile (uv.lock / Cargo.lock); CI matrix across all target OSes; signed release artifacts; single command bootstraps a working dev environment.

execution_sequence.phase_1_data_and_state: 1. Model the domain first, in a UI-free crate/package (core/): define entities, value objects, and enumerated state machines as types; make illegal states unrepresentable (Rust enums / Python tagged unions with exhaustive matching). No framework imports permitted in this layer — enforce with an import-linter contract (Python) or crate dependency graph (Rust). 2. Define the single application state tree: one root AppState aggregate, versioned, serializable, with every field owned by exactly one reducer/command handler. Document invariants as executable assertions. 3. Specify the mutation protocol before writing any mutation: state changes occur only through explicit Actions/Commands dispatched to the store; the store applies them serially (single writer), emits immutable snapshots or granular change notifications to subscribers. Direct field mutation from outside the store is a build failure, not a convention. 4. Design async state explicitly: every remote or long-running resource is modeled as a state machine (Idle → Loading → Loaded(data) | Failed(error)), never as a bare Optional/None that conflates "not yet" with "absent". Include cancellation tokens and staleness/epoch counters in the design. 5. Define persistence and migration: schema version embedded in all persisted state; forward migration functions written and tested alongside every schema change. 6. Exit criterion: the entire state layer is exercised by property-based tests (hypothesis/proptest) that dispatch random action sequences and verify invariants, with zero UI code in existence.
execution_sequence.phase_2_complex_logic: 1. Implement business logic as pure functions over domain types wherever possible: inputs and outputs only, effects returned as data (Command/Effect objects) and executed by a thin interpreter at the edge. This makes the complex core trivially testable and thread-agnostic. 2. Memory safety: in Rust, forbid unsafe in the core (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]); confine any required unsafe to a single audited module with documented invariants and Miri coverage. In Python, prevent leak-shaped patterns structurally: weak references for observer registrations, explicit lifecycle (close/aclose) on every resource via context managers, no module-level mutable caches without eviction policy. 3. Concurrency discipline: single-writer state store; all shared data crosses threads as immutable snapshots or through channels — never as shared mutable references. Every spawned task is owned (structured concurrency): Python asyncio.TaskGroup, Rust JoinSet — no fire-and-forget spawns. Every await point on external I/O carries a timeout and a cancellation path. 4. Backpressure: all queues and channels are bounded; define the overflow policy (drop-oldest, coalesce, or block-producer) per channel at design time. Event coalescing is mandatory for high-frequency producers (file watchers, tickers, progress streams). 5. Performance: establish criterion/pytest-benchmark baselines for the hot paths before optimizing; profile (perf/py-spy/tracing spans) before touching code; optimize allocation patterns (arena/pooling in Rust, avoiding per-frame object churn in Python) only where the profile proves it. Record budgets in the benchmark suite so regressions fail CI. 6. Error taxonomy: distinguish recoverable domain errors (typed, returned) from programmer errors (panic/assert) from environmental failures (retried with jittered exponential backoff and circuit breaking). No blanket exception swallowing; every error path either recovers meaningfully or propagates with context. 7. Exit criterion: core logic reaches its coverage and mutation-testing thresholds, passes race detection (loom for critical Rust lock-free sections; ThreadSanitizer where applicable; asyncio debug mode with slow-callback logging in Python), and meets benchmark budgets — all headless.
execution_sequence.phase_3_ui_integration: 1. Introduce a ViewModel/presenter layer that adapts store snapshots into render-ready view state (formatted strings, visibility flags, list deltas). Views bind to ViewModels only; ViewModels hold zero business logic and never touch I/O. 2. Threading contract: the UI thread does exactly three things — render, translate input events into dispatched Actions, and apply state-change notifications to widgets. All Action handling, I/O, and computation occur off-thread; results re-enter the UI thread solely via the framework's marshaling primitive (Qt queued signals / Tauri events / iced Command / egui context request-repaint). 3. Async bridging: wire the async runtime to the UI loop once, at startup, in one module (qasync loop policy; Tauri's managed tokio runtime; a dedicated runtime handle passed to iced/egui). Long operations dispatch Loading state immediately, stream progress via coalesced channel updates, and commit terminal state atomically. Every in-flight operation is cancellable from the UI and cancelled automatically on view teardown. 4. Staleness protection: tag every async response with the request epoch captured at dispatch; the reducer discards responses whose epoch does not match current state, eliminating out-of-order overwrite races from rapid user input. 5. Rendering discipline: virtualize all large collections (model/view with lazy fetch, not eager widget-per-row); batch and debounce store-to-UI notifications to at most one coalesced update per frame; keep per-frame allocations near zero on hot paths. 6. UI lifecycle hygiene: every subscription created on view construction is disposed on view destruction (RAII guards in Rust, context-managed connections or parent-owned QObject trees in Python); verify with a leak test that repeatedly opens and closes each view while asserting stable object counts. 7. Exit criterion: automated UI smoke tests (pytest-qt / WebDriver against Tauri / framework harness) prove that a deliberately slow (5 s) backend operation leaves the UI interactive, progress visible, and cancellation functional, with frame-time instrumentation showing no main-thread stall over budget.

critical_pitfalls.pitfall: Synchronous I/O, joins, or heavy computation on the render thread. Prevention: the UI layer is structurally forbidden from importing I/O modules; all work enters through the dispatch boundary; CI lint enforces the import contract.

Multiple writers mutating state concurrently, or async responses landing out of order. Prevention: single-writer store, message-passing over shared mutation, epoch-tagged responses, bounded channels; loom/TSan/property tests over interleavings.

Signal/callback subscriptions and closures capturing widgets or self, keeping dead views alive; Rust Rc/Arc reference cycles in callback graphs. Prevention: weak references for all observer registrations, scoped subscription guards disposed with the view, Weak for back-edges, open/close leak tests in CI.

Business logic reaching into widgets, or widgets querying databases. Prevention: enforced dependency direction UI → ViewModel → Store → Domain, with the domain depending on nothing; dependency inversion (traits/Protocols) for all effects; architecture conformance checked by tooling, not review vigilance.

Fire-and-forget tasks that outlive their owner, swallow exceptions, or write to torn-down views. Prevention: TaskGroup/JoinSet ownership everywhere, cancellation propagated on scope exit, a global assertion that no orphan tasks survive scene teardown.

High-frequency events flooding the UI or exhausting memory. Prevention: bounded channels with explicit overflow policy, coalescing/debouncing at every producer-consumer boundary, load-shedding metrics.
Using None/empty to mean both "loading" and "no data", causing flicker and phantom-empty bugs. Prevention: explicit Idle/Loading/Loaded/Failed state machines rendered exhaustively.
Optimizing without profiles, or caching without invalidation strategy. Prevention: benchmark baselines first, profile-guided changes only, every cache paired with an eviction and invalidation test.

Blanket except/catch that hides corruption and turns bugs into silent misbehavior. Prevention: typed error taxonomy, no bare excepts (lint-enforced), all unexpected errors surfaced to telemetry and the user-facing error boundary.

gate.question: Does the domain/core layer build and pass all tests with zero UI framework imports?
Is every state mutation routed through the single dispatch boundary, with direct external mutation impossible (compile error or lint failure)?
Do static checks pass at maximum strictness (mypy --strict and ruff clean; or cargo clippy -D warnings, rustfmt clean, forbid(unsafe_code) in core)?
Do property-based tests over random action sequences uphold all documented state invariants?
Is every async resource modeled as an explicit Idle/Loading/Loaded/Failed state machine, with exhaustive rendering of each variant?
Is every spawned task owned by a structured-concurrency scope, and does an automated test confirm zero orphan tasks and zero leaked subscriptions after view open/close cycles?
Does every external I/O call have a timeout, a cancellation path, and a tested failure branch?
Are all channels/queues bounded with an explicitly chosen and tested overflow policy?
Does the slow-backend UI test (5 s operation) demonstrate a responsive UI, visible progress, working cancellation, and no main-thread stall beyond the frame budget?
Do criterion/pytest-benchmark results meet the recorded performance budgets, with regression failure wired into CI?
Does a 24-hour (or CI-compressed equivalent) soak test show flat memory and no handle/file-descriptor growth?
Do race-detection tools (loom/TSan for Rust critical sections; asyncio debug and interleaving tests for Python) report zero findings on concurrent paths?
Is persisted state versioned, and does a test load every prior schema version through the migration chain successfully?
Are dependency lockfiles committed, licenses and security advisories audited (cargo-deny / pip-audit), and builds reproducible in CI across all target platforms?
Has a second engineer reviewed the change with the architecture conformance report (dependency direction, import contracts) attached and passing?
Do release artifacts build, sign, install, launch, and complete the smoke suite on every target OS?
